lesson.title: Sending Without Asking First
lesson.summary: A connectionless service model sends each unit of data independently with no prior handshake and no persistent session state, trading away guarantees about order or delivery for lower latency and lower overhead, which is exactly what UDP offers at the transport layer.
lesson.body:
A connectionless service model is the opposite choice from the connection oriented model covered just before this. Instead of establishing shared state before exchanging data, each unit of data, called a datagram, is sent as a fully self-contained message carrying its own destination information, with no handshake beforehand and no persistent state kept about the conversation afterward. Every datagram is handled independently by the network and by the receiving endpoint, which means datagrams can arrive out of order relative to how they were sent, can be duplicated, or can simply never arrive, and the connectionless protocol itself does nothing to detect or correct any of that.

UDP is the primary connectionless transport protocol on the internet, and IP itself, at the network layer, is also connectionless in exactly this sense, which is part of why UDP is often described as adding little more than port numbers on top of IP's own service model. A UDP sender simply addresses a datagram to a destination IP address and port and hands it to the network layer; there is no setup exchange like TCP's three way handshake, and no equivalent of a FIN based teardown, because there was never any connection state to close in the first place.

The advantages of this design are real and specific. Because there is no handshake, a connectionless exchange can complete in a single round trip instead of the multiple round trips a connection oriented protocol needs just to get started. Because there is no per-connection state to maintain, a server can field requests from an enormous number of distinct senders without allocating and tracking memory for each one individually. This matters enormously for protocols built around short, self-contained transactions, and it also matters for real time applications where holding onto a slow, retransmitted piece of old data is actually worse than simply losing it.

DNS is a clear worked example. A DNS query is typically a single small message asking a resolver to translate a hostname into an IP address, and the resolver's answer is typically a single small message in return. This is naturally a one round trip transaction, so sending it over UDP means the entire exchange, request and response, completes in one round trip, whereas doing the same thing over a connection oriented protocol would first require a handshake, at least doubling the time before the client ever receives an answer. Because most DNS queries fit in a single datagram and a lost query can simply be retried by the application, the lack of built-in reliability is an acceptable tradeoff for the latency saved.

Connectionless service does not mean chaotic or low quality; it means the guarantees are deliberately minimal, leaving decisions about retransmission, ordering, and session tracking to whatever layer above actually needs them. This framing sets up the next two concepts directly: best effort delivery describes exactly what happens, or does not happen, to a datagram once a connectionless protocol has sent it, and reliable delivery describes the opposite end of the spectrum, built specifically on top of connection oriented service.
